# Diagnosing High-Speed Engine Shutdown in Legacy ECUs

Encountering an engine cut-off event at 170 km/h on a 2005 Nissan Primera is a classic symptom of hardware degradation interacting with legacy firmware logic, rather than a sophisticated "safety feature" designed by modern manufacturers. While newer vehicles utilize complex CAN bus arbitration and redundant sensors to manage safety states, early-2000s ECUs often lacked the robust fault-handling mechanisms seen today. The fact that the car restarted successfully after cooling down suggests the issue is transient or thermal-dependent, pointing toward specific subsystems rather than a catastrophic mechanical failure like seized internals.

### Thermal Management and Fuel Delivery
The primary suspect in high-speed shutdown scenarios where overheating is ruled out is often the fuel delivery system. At 4600 rpm, the engine's demand for fuel spikes significantly. If the fuel pump is aging or if there is a restriction in the fuel lines, the ECU may detect a drop in fuel pressure that exceeds its safety thresholds and commands an immediate shutdown to prevent running out of fuel mid-injection cycle.

In modern diagnostic terms, this mimics a "low fuel pressure" fault code (often P0087). On older architectures like the Primera's, the ECU might not log a permanent fault if the condition resolves upon restart, leading to the behavior you observed: it works at 140 km/h but fails at 170 km/h. The update noting that the car turns off at high RPM even when stationary is a critical development. This indicates the fuel pump or its control circuit cannot sustain the required pressure regardless of load, suggesting mechanical wear in the pump's internal components or a failing relay.

### Ignition System Instability
The second major category for these symptoms is the ignition system. At high speeds, centrifugal force can cause worn distributor caps (if equipped) or coil packs to fail intermittently. However, since you mentioned the issue appears even when stationary at high RPM now, we must look closer at the spark plugs and wires. A failing plug wire that cannot handle the voltage spike at 4600 rpm will cause a misfire.

If the ECU detects excessive misfires (monitoring crankshaft position sensor signals), it will trigger a protective shutdown. This behavior is standard safety logic in ECUs from this era: if the engine isn't running smoothly, cut power to prevent damage to the catalytic converter or engine block. The observation that the car has a "lower probability" of shutting off after it hasn't happened recently suggests the component is on the brink of failure but not yet fully open-circuited.

### The Role of Legacy ECU Logic
You asked if this could be a programmed safety feature. In the context of 2005 technology, manufacturers did not program "safety features" that intentionally cut power at specific speeds unless a sensor threshold was breached. There is no firmware logic in an ECU that says "if speed > 170 km/h and RPM > 4000, stop engine." Such a feature would require real-time telemetry data processing capabilities that did not exist in mass-market vehicles of that generation.

The behavior you are seeingâwhere the car runs fine at 150 km/h but fails at 170 km/hâis almost certainly a threshold-based failure of a physical component. The ECU is reacting to a signal it interprets as dangerous: either insufficient fuel pressure or erratic ignition timing.

### Diagnostic Approach
Given that the issue has worsened to include shutdowns at stationary high RPM, the probability of simple thermal expansion causing the fault decreases, and mechanical failure increases. The most logical next step is not to push the speed limit higher but to inspect the fuel pump performance under load. You can attempt a voltage drop test across the fuel pump while cranking or running to see if the relay or wiring can sustain the amperage required at 4600 rpm.

If the fuel system checks out, the ignition coils and spark plugs are the next priority. Replacing these components is often more cost-effective than repairing an ECU that might be logging transient faults causing erratic behavior. While checking the ECU software is a valid engineering step, reflashing or modifying firmware on a 2005 unit without access to manufacturer-level diagnostic tools is rarely the solution for hardware-induced shutdowns.

### Final Recommendation
Do not attempt to drive faster than necessary until the root cause is identified. The progression from high-speed specific failure to stationary high-RPM failure indicates the system is losing stability under any high-load condition. Addressing the fuel or ignition components will likely restore the vehicle to its intended operating envelope without needing to investigate obscure sensor calibrations.
